paragraphs: Chayyab adam bikbod rabbo veyirato yoter mishshel abiv ki abiv hebio lechayye olam hazzeh verabbo mebio lechayye olam habba v"p sheyyesh omerim deim abiv hu rabbo mubhaq lo yiqraennu abi ella yiqraennu rabbi lo nahagu bekak ella apillu im abiv hu rabbo mubhaq yiqraennu abi veyesh taam lamminhag hazzeh:

clarification.explanation: A person is obligated in honoring and revering his teacher even more than his father, since his father brings him into life in this world, while his teacher brings him into life in the World to Come. Although some say that if one's father is also his primary teacher, he should not call him "my father" but "my teacher," the custom did not follow this, and even in this case he calls him "my father," and there is a reason for the custom.
takeaways: Honoring and revering one's teacher takes precedence over one's father, since the teacher brings one to the World to Come.
Even if one's father is also his primary teacher, he still calls him "my father."

paragraphs: Kol sherob chakemato mimmennu zeh niqra rabbo mubhaq vekol zeman sherabbo hammubhaq qayyam im qobea hattalmid midrash veyosheb vedoresh umelammed shello birshut rabbo "p shehu bimdina acheret hare zeh kecholeq al hashshekina abal muttar lachaloq alayv beezeh pasaq o horaa im yesh lo reayot vehokachot lidbarayv shehaddin ken dekol shehu derek massa umattan shari umihu lo yachaloq kederek hacholeqim lanetzach ella omer reayotayv veim yasheru beenayv mutab veim lav yishtoq veken liktob leatzmo reayotayv ap shehem keneged rabbo muttar abal liktob pasaq o horaa neged rabbo umoser laacherim asur veim nechlequ hachakamim veamedu leminyan lo yimneh keneged rabbo im hacholeqim alayv vekol zeh bechayyayv abal acher muttar muttar lachaloq alayv velipsoq kepi sebarato velaasot maaseh ap shehu keneged rabbo abal lo yomar rabbi haya omer kak vaani omer kak shezzeh mebazzeh et rabbo ak yukal liktob sebarat rabbo ureayotayv veyiktob alayv dibre atzmo ureayotayv "p shehem soterim ki haroeh dibrehem yibchar veken asu kol harishonim veal hakkol yihyu debarayv leshem shamayim kak katab haggaon haradba"z za"l vehebi debarayv harab birke yosep za"l ot g' vesham heir harab za"l miggemara derosh hashshana dap y"ch ammud b' deamar rabbi shimon arbaa debarim haya doresh rabbi aqiba veen ani doresh kemoto veku' venirin debaray middebarayv verabbi shimon talmid rabbi aqiba hava vekatab aggada shane, vedibre haradba"z bahalaka lemaaseh sheoseh neged rabbo vezeh zilzul lerabbo upashut ad kan debarayv veharoeh yireh deachar mechila rabba lo heela mazor lehearato bazeh hachilluq. veli ana abda nireh li, dibrabbu hammubhaq, gam baaggada en lemor ken kemo sheamar rabbi shimon bar yochay ak hachilluq hu dekol zeh emor berabbo mubhaq sherob chakemato mimmennu abal rabbi aqiba "g dehu rabba derashbi"y lo hayeta rob chakemato shel rashbi"y mimmennu kede sheyyihyeh lo din rabbo mubhaq shetztzarik lehizzaher bekol elleh. od ana abada hairoti beha ditnan besop pereq g' dikratut: amar rabbi aqiba: shaalti et rabbi eliezer, haoseh veku' amar li: chayyab al kol achat veachat miqqal vachomer veku' amarti lo im amarta bannidda veku' amar lo habe veku' amarti lo lo im amarta babba veku' veek yomar lo, sheddocheh debarayv belashon zeh vahalo ita besanhedrin (dap po.) deamar rab yehuda lerab yechezqel abiv la titteni haki vehokicho shemuel veamar lo la tema laabuk haki veteratzti derabbi aqiba lo haya rob chakemato min rabbi eliezer, velaken let lah din rabbo mubhaq velaken gam lerabbi yehoshua amar lo rabbi aqiba beoto happereq hannizkar (keritot tv:) im halaka neqabbel veim laddin yesh teshuba degam rabbi yehoshua eno niqra rabbi mubhaq dela have rob chakemato mimmennu veayyen bipsachim pereq shishshi (dap sv.) mah sheheshib rabbi aqiba al dibre rabbi eliezer veita birushalmi sham halaka g' shelosha asar shana niknas rabbi aqiba bebet midrasho shel rabbi eliezer lilmod tora mimmennu velo haya yodea bo rabbi eliezer velo hechshibu vezo hatteshuba shel hazzaa tokicha, hayeta teshuba rishona sheheshib rabbi aqiba al dibre rabbi eliezer veimma lo rabbi yehoshua lerabbi eliezer halo zeh haam asher maasta bo tze na atta vehillachem bo ayyen sham ubemaqom acher katabti bazeh bs"d:

clarification.explanation:
A "primary teacher" is one from whom most of the student's wisdom comes. As long as the primary teacher lives, a student who establishes his own study hall and sits, expounds, and teaches without his teacher's permission — even in another country — is considered as though disputing the Divine Presence. But it is permitted to disagree with him on a particular ruling or instruction if one has proofs and evidence that the law is so, since anything done in the manner of Torah discussion is permitted — provided he does not argue in the manner of those who argue to win, but states his proofs; if accepted, good, and if not, he should remain silent. He may write down his proofs for himself even if they contradict his teacher, but it is forbidden to write a ruling or instruction against his teacher and hand it to others; and if the sages disputed and were counted for a vote, he should not be counted against his teacher among those who disagree with him. All this applies during his teacher's lifetime, but after his death it is permitted to disagree with him, to rule according to his own reasoning, and even to act against his teacher's view; only he should not say "my teacher used to say this and I say that," since this demeans his teacher, but should write his teacher's reasoning and proofs, and after them his own words and proofs, even though they contradict, and let the reader choose — and so did all the early authorities. Above all, his words should be for the sake of Heaven. All this is from the words of the Gaon Radbaz, cited by Rabbi Berachi Yosef.

The Berachi Yosef raised a difficulty from the Gemara in Rosh Hashanah: Rabbi Shimon said, "Rabbi Akiva expounded four things and I do not expound them like him... and my words seem more correct than his" — yet Rabbi Shimon was Rabbi Akiva's student! He resolved that in matters of Aggadah the law is different, and the Radbaz's words were said regarding practical halacha, where acting against one's teacher demeans him. Rabbi Yosef Chaim writes that, with all due respect, this distinction does not fully resolve the difficulty, and offers another resolution: regarding a truly primary teacher, one should not say this even in Aggadah; rather, Rabbi Akiva, although he was Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's teacher, was not the source of most of Rashbi's wisdom, and therefore did not carry for him the status of a primary teacher requiring all these precautions.

In this way Rabbi Yosef Chaim resolves an additional difficulty: in the Mishnah at the end of the third chapter of Keritot, Rabbi Akiva rejects Rabbi Eliezer's words with the language "No, if you said..." — how did he reject his words with such language, when in Sanhedrin Samuel rebuked Rav Yehuda for saying to his father "you should not teach it this way," teaching him not to speak to his father this way? Rather, Rabbi Akiva did not receive most of his wisdom from Rabbi Eliezer, and therefore he did not carry for him the status of a primary teacher; for the same reason he also said to Rabbi Yehoshua in the same chapter, "if it is a received tradition we accept it, but if it is a legal argument there is a response" — since Rabbi Yehoshua too was not his primary teacher. And proof from the Jerusalem Talmud in Pesachim: for thirteen years Rabbi Akiva entered Rabbi Eliezer's study hall to learn Torah from him, and Rabbi Eliezer did not know him or regard him; and the response "let sprinkling prove it" was his first response to Rabbi Eliezer's words, "is this not the people you rejected — go now and fight them."
takeaways: A "primary teacher" is one from whom most of the student's wisdom comes; one should not establish an independent teaching post during his lifetime without permission.
It is permitted to disagree through Torah proofs, not to win — remaining silent if not accepted.
After the teacher's death, one may rule by his own reasoning, but should not say "my teacher said X, I say Y" — rather record both views.
One whose wisdom did not mostly come from a certain teacher does not owe him the laws of a primary teacher (like Rabbi Akiva with Rabbi Eliezer).

paragraphs: Kol haoseh meriba im rabbo hammubhaq keoseh im hashshekina vekol hammitraem alayv vehamharher acharayv keillu mitraem umeharher achar hashshekina vehay issura dimharher lav bemachshaba ella hakkavvana bazeh lomar shehu medabber umechappeh alayv debarim veayyen birke yosep ot b':

clarification.explanation: Anyone who quarrels with his primary teacher is as though quarreling with the Divine Presence, and anyone who complains about him or harbors suspicion against him is as though complaining and harboring suspicion against the Divine Presence. The prohibition of "harboring suspicion" here is not merely in thought, but means speaking and casting accusations against him.
takeaways: Quarreling or complaining about one's teacher is like quarreling with the Divine Presence.
The prohibition includes speech and casting accusations against him, not merely private thought.

paragraphs: Asur liqboa atzmo lehoraa lehorot beqeba apillu rachoq merabbo hammubhaq mahalak kamma yamim ella im ken natan lo rabbo reshut veim natan lo reshut yakol lehorot apillu bepanayv veyesh omerim dilpanayv mammash asur vela miqqere horaa ella kishmura al maaseh shebba lepanayv abal im sheellu oto halaka sheenah leinyan maaseh yukal lomar mah shebbedato vaapillu im moreh al maaseh eno ella bedabar sheyyesh bo chiddush lashshoel, abal behoraa yedua sheppeshuta lekol kegon noten taam lipgam o lebattel issur beshishshim vekayyotze muttar apillu beli netilat reshut veyesh mi shekkatab dekol hakkatub basseparim mippisqe haggeonim yukal lehorot beli netilat reshut raq lo yoreh dabar millibbo velo yismok al atzmo ledammot milleta lemilleta vbsh"q mqbtzyl heeleti dekol din sheppasequ maran za"l beshulchano hattahor sheqqibbalnu horaotayv yakol lehorot beli netilat reshut uleaproshe meissura kegon sheroeh adam oseh issur yakol lomar lo shehu asur bipne rabbo shebbekol maqom sheyyesh chillul hashshem en choleqin kabod larab:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden for a student to establish himself as a permanent teaching authority, even several days' journey from his primary teacher, unless his teacher gave him permission. And if he gave him permission, he may teach even directly in his teacher's presence, though some disagree, holding that teaching directly in the teacher's presence is forbidden even with permission. Forbidden "instruction" (according to all views) applies only when ruling on an actual case brought before him, but if he was asked a halacha not for practical application, or a simple instruction known to all (such as "imparting a spoiling taste" or nullification in sixty), it is permitted even without taking permission. And any law Maran ruled in the Shulchan Aruch, he may instruct without permission. And to separate a person from a prohibition (when seeing him transgressing), it is permitted to tell him it is forbidden even in the teacher's presence, since where there is desecration of God's name, one does not defer honor to the teacher.
takeaways: A student may not establish himself as a permanent teaching authority without his teacher's permission, even far away.
Even with permission, some hold teaching directly in the teacher's presence is forbidden.
Instruction on a simple, universally known matter, or an explicit Shulchan Aruch ruling, is permitted without permission.
Separating a person from a prohibition is permitted in any case, even before the teacher, since desecration of God's name overrides deference.

paragraphs: Asur letalmid liqrot lerabbo hammubhaq bishmo bilbad lo bechayyayv velo bemoto ella yomar rabbi peloni vaapillu liqrot laacherim sheshshemam kishmo asur im hu shem pile sheen hakkol regilin bo:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden for a student to call his primary teacher by his name alone, neither during his life nor after his death, but should say "Rabbi so-and-so." And it is even forbidden to call another person who shares his teacher's name by that name alone, if it is a rare name not commonly used by all.
takeaways: One does not call a teacher by his name alone, but "Rabbi so-and-so."
Care is taken even with a rare name shared by another person identical to the teacher's.

paragraphs: Lo yitten shalom lerabbo hammubhaq velo yachazor lo shalom kederek shear haam ella shocheh lepanayv veomer lo beyira ubekabod shalom aleka rabbi veim natan lo rabbo shalom omer lo shalom aleka rabbi umori:

clarification.explanation: One should not greet his primary teacher or return his greeting the way one does with ordinary people, but should bow before him and say with reverence and honor, "Peace upon you, my teacher." And if his teacher greeted him, he responds, "Peace upon you, my teacher and my master."
takeaways: One greets and returns a greeting to his teacher with a bow, honor, and reverence, in a special formula.

paragraphs: Lo yachalotz tepillin lipne rabbo hammubhaq velo yaseb lepanayv ella yosheb keyosheb lipne hammelek velo yitpallel lepanayv velo leacharayv velo betziddo mammash vekol shekken deasur lelek betziddo vechutz learba ammot hakkol shari velo yesheb lepanayv ad sheyyomar lo sheb velo yaamod lelek ad sheyyittol reshut mimmennu ukesheyyiptor millepanayv lo yachazir lo achorayv:

clarification.explanation: One should not remove tefillin in his primary teacher's presence, nor recline before him, but should sit as one sits before a king. He should not pray before him, behind him, or directly beside him, and all the more so it is forbidden to walk beside him, but outside four cubits everything is permitted. He should not sit until his teacher tells him to sit, should not stand to leave until he takes permission, and when parting from him should not turn his back to him.
takeaways: One conducts oneself before a teacher as before a king: sitting with awe, not turning one's back when parting.
One does not sit, stand, or pray directly beside the teacher without permission.

paragraphs: Lo yesheb bimqomo velo yakria debarayv velo yiptor debarayv apillu bemille dealema vechayyab laamod mippanayv mishsheyyirennu merachoq melo enayv ad sheyyitkasseh mimmennu o ad sheyyesheb vaapillu haya rabbo rokeb tzarik laamod mippanayv dachashib kimhallek vekol mealakot shehaebed oseh lerabbo talmid oseh lerabbo:

clarification.explanation: He should not sit in his teacher's designated place, and should not decide or rule between his words, nor contradict his words, even in mundane matters. He must stand for his teacher from the moment he sees him from as far as his eyes can see, until he is hidden from view or sits down. Even if his teacher is riding, one must stand for him, since this is considered like walking, and every task a servant does for his master, a student does for his teacher.
takeaways: One does not sit in the teacher's place or decide/contradict his words.
One stands for him as long as he is visible, and serves him like a servant serves his master.

paragraphs: Raa rabbo ober al dibre tora apillu issur derabbanan omer lo kak limmadtanu rabbenu ubeshemmazkir et rabbo tok y"b chodesh tzarik lemor horani kapparat mishkabo veim raq bipne rabbo hu biklal "kol mesanay ahabu mavet" ella yistalleq mishsham veyaroq o yeballeennu biksuto veyesh mattirin beroq bealema veen oserin ella bekicho shehu dabar sheyyotze miggupo bekoach vetzarik lachush ledibre haoserim apillu beroq bealema:

clarification.explanation: If he saw his teacher transgressing the words of the Torah, even a rabbinic prohibition, he should say to him respectfully, "Is this not what you taught us, our teacher?" And when mentioning his teacher within twelve months of his passing, he should say, "I am an atonement for his resting place." It is forbidden to spit in his teacher's presence, but he should leave the area, and if compelled, he should swallow the saliva into his garment. One should be stringent about this even with ordinary saliva.
takeaways: One rebukes a teacher with the language "Is this not what you taught us?"
One says "I am an atonement for his resting place" within a year of his death, and does not spit in his presence.

paragraphs: Kol ellu haddebarim sheamarnu shetztzarik lekabbed bahem et rabbo lo neemru ella berabbo mubhaq davqa sherob chakemato mimmennu im miqra miqra veim mishna mishna veim gemara gemara abal im en rob chakemato mimmennu eno tzarik lekabbedo bekol elleh haddebarim sheamarnu abal omed millepanayv mishsheyyaggia learba ammetayv, veken nakon name keshemmazkir shemo yomar rabbi peloni:

clarification.explanation: All these laws of honor apply specifically to a primary teacher, from whom most of one's wisdom comes — whether in Scripture, Mishnah, or Gemara. But one whose wisdom did not mostly come from a certain person need not honor him in all these ways, but only stands for him when he comes within four cubits, and it is proper, when mentioning his name, to say "Rabbi so-and-so."
takeaways: The full laws of honor apply only to a primary teacher, from whom most wisdom comes.
A non-primary teacher: one stands within four cubits and calls him "Rabbi."

paragraphs: "g deamerinan dechayyab laamod bipne rabbo "p sheeno rabbo mubhaq mikkol maqom im zeh rabbo shellamedu min ale"p be"t ad gemar hattana"k abal lo lamedu gemara vetora shb"p mippene shezzeh hamlammed eno yodea lilmod gemara vehalak zeh hattalmid velamad gemara lipne rab acher venaasa talmid chakam chashub eno chayyab zeh betalmid laamod lipne zeh hamlammed "p shellamedu kol hammiqra kullah yaan ki zeh hamlammed nechshab atta legabbe zeh hattalmid chakam leamma deara, veek zeh shehu chakam ubaal horaa yaqum mippanayv ki ziluta letalmid chakam laqum bipne hedyot vekol shekken im zeh hamlammed shellamedu kol hammiqra kullah lo lemado bechinnam ella limmedu besakar demechamat ken name betzir leh yeqareh al ken eno qam mippanayv umikkol maqom rauy laasot lo hiddur velinhog bo ezeh kabod vehaki have sugyan dealema ukemo shekkatab haggaon chida" za"l bebirke yosep ubeshiyyure beraka yeuyyan sham veellu hamon haam shellomedim tana"k umeat midreshe rz"l beaggada lipne melammede tinoqot veyotzeim lashshuq laasaqim veen lomedim yoter denimtza zeh haadam kol chakemato vidiato battora o rubbah hu min hamlammed hazzeh chashib hamlammed hazzeh rabbo mubhaq vechayyab linhog bo kol hilkot rabbo mubhaq shekketanu deal zeh katab maran za"l beshulchano hattahor bedin rabbo mubhaq sherob chakemato mimmennu im miqra miqqera veim mishna mishna upashut:

clarification.explanation: Although one must stand even before a non-primary teacher, one who was taught only Scripture (the alphabet through the end of the Bible) but not Gemara, and the student went and studied Gemara with another teacher and became an important Torah scholar — he is not obligated to stand before that first teacher, since the teacher is now considered, relative to him, an unlearned person, and it is disrespectful for a Torah scholar to stand before an ordinary layman, especially if he taught him for pay. Nevertheless, it is proper to treat him with honor and respect. But for the common people whose entire Torah wisdom, or most of it, comes from the teacher (who taught them Scripture and a little Aggadah before they went into business), the teacher is considered their primary teacher and they are obligated in all the laws of a primary teacher.
takeaways: A Torah scholar whose teacher only taught him Scripture need not stand for him, though should treat him respectfully.
For one whose entire wisdom comes from the teacher, the teacher is a primary teacher.

paragraphs: Ketib mippene seba taqum vehadarta pene zaqen vehaynu shiba adam shehu ben shibim shana vezaqen zeh hechakam sheqqana chakema vegam hannashim chayyabot bemitzva zo laqum mippene hazzaqen umippene hechakam vaapillu im hazzaqen am haaretz tzarik laqum mippanayv ubilbad shello yihyeh rasha velaken ellu habbiryonim sheyyodea bahem sheen mitpallelin bekol yom veenam mannichin tepillin eno chayyab laqum mippenehem kelal ki al zaqen kazeh lo tzivveta hattora lekabbedo v"g dekatabnu shechiyyub mitzvat aseh laqum mippene zaqen haynu ben shibim shana kol zeh hu kepi dibre happoseqim happashtanim abal lepi daat rabbenu haari"y za"l tzarik laqum bipne hazzaqen mibben shishshim shana vamala vetzarik lehizzaher bazeh ki debarayv neemanim al pi hassod dibre elohe chayyim:

clarification.explanation: It is said, "You shall rise before gray hair and honor the presence of an elder" — "gray hair" refers to one seventy years old, and "an elder" is a scholar who has acquired wisdom. Women too are obligated in this commandment to stand before an elder and a scholar. Even an unlearned elder requires standing, provided he is not wicked — therefore those who cast off the yoke, who do not pray and do not don tefillin, need not be stood for. According to the plain reading, the obligation begins at seventy, but according to the Arizal, one must stand from age sixty and above, and one should be careful about this according to the mystical tradition.
takeaways: One stands before an elder (seventy) and a scholar; women too are obligated.
One does not stand before a wicked elder; the Arizal holds the obligation begins at sixty.

paragraphs: Meematay chayyab adam laqum mippenehem mishsheyyaggiu letok arba ammotayv ad sheyyaabru mikkeneged panayv o yashebu veim rotzeh laqum mippene hazzaqan o hechakam qodem sheyyaggiu tok arba ammotayv eno rashshay veayyen mim shekkatabti bs"d bsh"q rab berakot bemaareket hap' ot ' yeuyyan sham veyesh lehistappeq im niknesu hechakam o hazzaqan lebet hakkeneset o lechatzer hammuqqap i amerinan kol habbayit chashib kearba ammot vechayyab laqum "p shehem bau veyashebu rachoq min haadam hayyosheb sham yoter min d' ammot, o dilma, gam bazeh yesh din arba ammot hannizkar veayyen mah shekkatab haggaon chida" za"l bebirke yosep venireh li kevan dehave sepeqa deorayeta azelinan lechumera vetzarik laqum mippenehem "p sheyyeshebu rachoq mimmennu mihu im hu yodea shehem baim lehitqareb lesheb samuk lo lo yaqum mippenehem ella ad sheyyaggiu letok arba ammotayv ken heeleti bsh"q mqbtzyl bs"d: od heeleti sham bs"d deim haadam yosheb bebeto lemala beaksadra shehi gabohha ureshut bipne atzmah vehazzaqan o hechakam niknesu lechatzer veyashebu lematta samuk laaksadra velo alu lemala leaksadra deeno chayyab laqum kevan dehu yosheb birshut bipne atzmah, veen zo qima sheyyesh bah hiddur. abal im hu yosheb babbima asher beemtza bet hakkeneset vehem holekim lematta bebet hakkeneset uqerobim labbima yaqum mippenehem yaan ki din bima asher bebet hakkeneset qayma lan debatela hi legabbe bet hakkeneset veenah nechshebet reshut bipne atzmah beinyan hatztzerup kemo shekkatabti behilkot bet hakkeneset.

clarification.explanation: One must stand for an elder or a scholar from the moment they come within four cubits until they pass from view or sit down, and if one wishes to stand before they reach four cubits, this is not proper. If the scholar or elder entered the synagogue and sat more than four cubits away, out of doubt (a Torah-level doubt) one should be stringent and stand, unless one knows they are approaching to sit nearby — in which case one stands only when they reach within four cubits. And if he sits in a separate, elevated area while they are below, he need not stand, since this is not a standing that carries proper respect; but one sitting on the platform in the middle of the synagogue stands for them, since the platform is considered part of the synagogue.
takeaways: One stands within the four-cubit range until they pass or sit — not before.
Entering the synagogue — one should be stringent and stand; a separate, elevated area exempts one.

paragraphs: Apillu im hechakam o hazzaqan rokebim ben al behema ben baagala tzarik laqum mippenehem veayin t"z, siman rm"b seip qatan y" vehattora hizhira sheasur laatzom enayv min hechakam o hazzaqen beodennu rachoq mimmennu kede shello yaqum kesheyyaggia letok d' ammotayv delaken ketib bemitzva zo veyareta meeloheka hayyodea machashabot leb:

clarification.explanation: Even if the scholar or elder is riding, whether on an animal or in a carriage, one must stand for them. And the Torah warned that it is forbidden to close one's eyes to avoid seeing the scholar or elder while still far away, so as not to have to stand when they reach four cubits — and therefore it is said regarding this commandment, "and you shall fear your God," who knows the thoughts of the heart.
takeaways: One stands even for a scholar or elder who is riding.
It is forbidden to pretend not to have seen them in order to avoid standing.

paragraphs: Apillu beshaa sheoseq battora chayyab laamod bipne hechakam o hazzaqen veillu bebet hakkeneset vaapillu bishat tepilla kesheqqore zemirot veyotzer uqeriat shema shezzehu kebodo yitbarek ki hu amar vayyehi hu tzivva vayyaamod lipne hechakam vehazzaqan ukemo shekkatab harab za"l sham mihu im haomed hu saggi nehor nistappeq bazeh nachalat tzebi vehinnicha betzarik iyyun yeuyyan sham ubevadday tzarik laqum dispeq tora lehachmir vekol shekken beha dehassebara nota sheyyaqum:

clarification.explanation: Even while engaged in Torah study, one must stand before the scholar or elder, and likewise in the synagogue even while reciting hymns, Yotzer, or the Shema — since it is also God's honor when a person stands before the scholar and elder whom He commanded to honor. Even a blind person, although there is doubt about this, should stand, since a Torah-level doubt is resolved stringently, and reasoning also leans toward standing.
takeaways: One stands for a scholar or elder even during Torah study and prayer.
Even a blind person should stand, since a Torah-level doubt is resolved stringently.

paragraphs: Yesh omerim deeshet chaber dinah kechaber leinyan zeh latztzarik laqum mippaneha veyesh omerim deeno chayyab middina ella mimmiddat chasidut venakon lachush lisbara rishona velaqum veayyen birke yosep choshen mishpat siman tv"b ot Adonai yeuyyan sham veharab hannizkar bebirke yosep yoreh dea, katab sherabbenu haari"y ztz"l katab deen chiyyub laamod lipne eshet talmid chakam vegam lo laasot lah hiddur yeuyyan sham vaana abda lo yadati hekan raa harab za"l dabar zeh bedibre haari"y za"l dibshaar hammitzvot katab veza"l ubeishsha neemar veyareta meeloheka yireh balleb veen tzarik lah lo qima velo hiddur ad kan leshono udebarayv ellu qae al ishsha zeqena veishsha chakema abal eshet talmid chakam chiyyub qima gabbah hu mishshum kebod balah shehi kegupo vachashib keillu hem qamim bipne balah vezeh pashut veda daapillu man disbira lehu eshet chaber kechaber leinyan zeh mikkol maqom modeh dela amerinan eshet zaqen kezaqen dikbod tora shane vezeh pashut ubarur;

clarification.explanation: Some say the wife of a scholar has the law of a scholar and one must stand for her, and some say there is no obligation by strict law, only as a measure of piety, and it is proper to be concerned for the first view and stand. The obligation to stand for her is due to her husband's honor, since she is like his own body, as though standing before her husband. Nevertheless, even those who hold a scholar's wife has the law of a scholar agree that one does not say an elder's wife has the law of an elder, since the honor of Torah is different.
takeaways: It is proper to stand for a Torah scholar's wife, due to her husband's honor.
There is no law of "an elder's wife like an elder" — the honor of Torah is distinct.

paragraphs: En omedin lo bebet hakkisse velo bebet hammerchatz diktib taqum vehadarta qima sheyyesh bah biddur abal babbayit hachitzon shel hammerchatz omedin veen baale ummanuyot chayyabe laamod bipne hechakam o hazzaqen beshaa sheoseqin bimlaaktam veim rotzeh lehachmir al atzmo velaamod rashshay abal im hu sekir yom sheoseq bimleket acherim eno rashshay lehechamer vequm vekatab hakkeneset haggedola beshem harab rabbenu abraham hallevi za"l. daapillu bipne rabbo hammubhaq eno chayyab laqum kesheoseq bimlakto:

clarification.explanation: One does not stand before a scholar or elder in the outhouse or the bathhouse, since it is said, "you shall rise and honor" — a standing that carries proper respect; but in the outer room of the bathhouse, one does stand. Craftsmen are not obligated to stand while engaged in their work, and if one wishes to be stringent and stand, he may, but a daily wage laborer engaged in others' work may not be stringent and stand. Even before his own primary teacher, he is not obligated to stand while engaged in his work.
takeaways: One does not stand in the outhouse or the inner bathhouse.
A craftsman is exempt while working; a daily wage laborer may not even be stringent and stand.

paragraphs: Apillu chakam omed bipne hazzaqan ak eno chayyab laqum male qomato ella kede lehaddero veken shene chakamim ushene zeqenim en echad tzarik laqum male qumu ella yaasu hiddur zeh lazeh veim rotzim laqum rashshaim veken harab letalmido yaaseh lo hayder qetzat:

clarification.explanation: Even a scholar stands before an elder, but need not stand to his full height, only enough to show him respect. Likewise two scholars, or two elders, need not stand to full height for one another, but should show each other respect (and if they wish to stand fully, they may). And even a teacher shows his student a small measure of respect.
takeaways: A scholar stands for an elder, but only enough to show respect, not to full height.
Two equals show each other respect; a teacher shows his student a small measure too.

paragraphs: Chakam apillu muplag bechakema rashshay laamod bipne adam baal maasim veyesh omerim sheyyesh chiyyub laamod bipne baal maasim venakon laamod bipne gabbay tzedaqa beshaa sheggobin, veken bipne kol oseh mitzva beshaa sheosin. vedavqa im osin bechinnam abal im osin besakar en chayyabin laamod bipnehem venahagu poh irenu bagdad y" im adam yosheb bebeto veyodea shemmolikin hammet barechob shekkeneged beto umelavvin oto sheyyaqumu kol anshe habbayit veyaamdu melo qomatam betok betam ad sheyyaabru kol hamlavvin meoto rechob shekkeneged habbayit hahu:

clarification.explanation: A scholar, even one of great distinction, may stand before a person of good deeds, and some say there is an obligation in this. It is proper to stand for charity collectors while they are collecting, and likewise before anyone performing a commandment while performing it — specifically when done for free, not for pay. In Baghdad it was customary that a person sitting at home who knows a funeral is passing in the street facing his house — all household members would stand to their full height until all the mourners had passed.
takeaways: It is proper to stand for a person of good deeds, charity collectors, and those performing commandments for free.
In Baghdad, households stood fully while a funeral passed by in the street.

paragraphs: "p deameru rabbotenu za"l (megilla kch:) asur lehishtammesh bemi sheshshoneh halakot haynu davqa shimmush shel abdut kegon hak deresh laqish shennaseu al ketepo o kehak dibamot dap m"b ammud b' demistemik veazel rabbi abboahh akkatpeh derabbi nachum shammaeh abal shimmush sheragil adam laasot lachabero bederek gemilut chesed eno biklal zeh. deim lo ken lo matzanu yadenu veraglenu leqabbel shimmush mibbene tora meachar sheen etzlenu talmid sherob chakemato merabbo kevan shellomedim mehasseparim, ken katab harab binyan tziyyon za"l besi' p"g yeuyyan sham:

clarification.explanation: Although the Sages said it is forbidden to make use of one who studies halachot, this applies specifically to servile use (such as carrying him on one's shoulder or leaning on him), but ordinary service one person does for another as an act of kindness is not included in this prohibition — otherwise we could not accept any service from Torah scholars, since in our time there is no student whose wisdom mostly comes from his teacher, as people learn from books.
takeaways: It is forbidden to make servile use of a Torah scholar, but ordinary kindly service is permitted.

paragraphs: Mitzvat aseh al haish lelammed et beno tora ukeshem shemmitzva lelammed et beno kak mitzva lelammed et ben beno diktib (debarim d, t) "vehodatam lebaneka velibne baneka" vechayyab lehaskir melammed kede lelammed et beno veet ben beno vei la tzayet liskor kayepinan leh. veim eno bair veyesh lo nekasim i epshar leodee leh, modiin leh veim lav bet din yoredin linkasayv vesokerin melammed libno o leben beno:

clarification.explanation: It is a positive commandment for a man to teach his son Torah, and just as it is a commandment to teach his son, so it is a commandment to teach his grandson, as it is said, "and you shall make them known to your children and your children's children." He must hire a teacher to teach his son and his grandson, and if he does not wish to hire one, he is compelled. And if he is not in the city and has assets, if possible he is notified, and if not, the court draws from his assets and hires a teacher for his son or grandson.
takeaways: It is a commandment to teach one's son and grandson Torah, and to hire a teacher.
One who does not is compelled; the court may draw from his assets to hire a teacher.

paragraphs: Mishsheyyatchil ledabber melammedo abiv pasuq shema yisrael veku' upasuq tora tzivva lanu mosheh upasuq baruk Adonai leolam amen veamen vegam melammedo laanot amen al habberakot vekaasher yatchil lelammedo miqra bebet hasseper yatchil lelammedo min parashat vayyiqra deameru rabbotenu za"l yabou tahoram veyitassequ bitharot. veayyen seper chasidim siman ttsh"m veyishtaddel lelammedo birkot hannehenin ubirkat asher yatzar beal peh vegam qeriat shema veyargilu lilmod qeriat shema babboqer ubaereb al hammitta velo yannichu lishon beli qeriat shema ubazeh yihyeh lo toelet harbeh leyirat shamayim lebassop:

clarification.explanation: From when the child begins to speak, his father teaches him verses: "Hear O Israel," "Moses commanded us the Torah," and "Blessed is the Lord forever, Amen and Amen," and also teaches him to answer Amen to blessings. And when he begins to study Scripture at school, they begin with Parashat Vayikra — "let the pure come and engage with pure things." He should endeavor to teach him orally the blessings over enjoyment, the blessing "Asher Yatzar," and the Shema, and get him accustomed to reciting the Shema morning and evening at bedtime, never sleeping without it, through which he will ultimately merit fear of Heaven.
takeaways: A child is taught opening verses and to answer Amen.
Scripture study begins with Vayikra; the child is trained in the Shema and blessings by heart.

paragraphs: Yaskir lo melammed piqqeach shemmakkir beseder hallimmud im yeladim lepi tiban vegam sheyyihyeh medaqdeq heteb ki girsa deyanquta la tishtakkach vegam sheyyihyeh neeman shello yaaseh meleket Adonai remiyya vegam sheyyihyeh mashgicha al hayyeladim leshameram mikkol maaseh kiur veissur vegam yashgicha heteb alehem bahalikatam lebet hakkisse veyashgicha shello yityachadu immahem bene adam sheenam mehugganim ki hayyeladim yitpattu benaqel velo amon bam vehamlammed im yesh lo taanit yartzayt lo yitanneh vekol shekken shear taaniyyot shel nedaba ki bazeh memaet meleket shamayim shebbeyado veim adam roeh sheen hamlammed mitnaheg kashshura velimmudo mequlqal yiqqach beno miyyado veyannichennu etzel melammed acher velo yihyeh lo rachamanut al hamlammed bishbil parnasato ki bazeh hu mitakzer al beno vechote lelohim:

clarification.explanation: He should hire a shrewd teacher for his son who knows how to order study for children according to their nature, is very meticulous (since a child's learning is never forgotten), is trustworthy not to cheat in his work, and watches over the children to guard them from anything forbidden or unseemly — including when they go to the outhouse, and that unsuitable people not be alone with them, since children are easily lured. The teacher should not observe fasts (even a yahrzeit, and certainly a voluntary fast), so as not to diminish the sacred work in his hands. And if he sees the teacher not conducting himself properly, he should remove his son from him and not spare him out of concern for his livelihood, since this would be cruel to his own son.
takeaways: One should choose a shrewd, meticulous, trustworthy teacher who watches over the children.
A teacher should not fast; an improper teacher should be replaced, without regard for his livelihood.

paragraphs: Hamlammed yizdarez lelammed et hayladim shaa achat bayyom hilkot derek eretz vedibre musar chanok lannaar al pi darko vibaer lahem hakketubim battana"k beharchaba lepi hashgachatam vedatam shello yihyu hakketubim bepihem kezemer bealema sheen mebinim ma hem haddebarim sheyyotziu mippihem vekaasher yetargem lahem hammiqra bilshon hammedina yizzaher ledaqdeq ballashon hahu sheyyihyeh metuqqan bimqomot hatztzerikin tiqqun kol dabar lepi inyano:

clarification.explanation: The teacher should hasten to teach the children one hour a day the laws of proper conduct and words of ethical instruction — "train a child according to his way" — and should explain the verses of Scripture to them extensively according to their understanding, so the verses are not merely a chant in their mouths without understanding. And when translating Scripture for them into the vernacular, he should be careful to be precise in language and correction where needed, each matter according to its nature.
takeaways: Teachers should devote an hour daily to ethics and proper conduct, and explain verses thoroughly.
One must ensure the child understands the material, and be precise in translation.

paragraphs: Hamlammed tinoqot eno rashshay letargem megillat shir hashshirim belashon arbi o shear leshonot kepi mashmaut hammillot mammash bilbad yaan ki debarim asher bimgillat shir hashshirim lo neemru kepi peshutan mammash ella raq nittenu lehiddaresh bilbad. velaken timtza baal hattargum lo tirgem megillat shir hashshirim kishar targumim shehem targume hammillot bipshutan ella hebi al kol pasuq dibre midrash yaan ki peshutan hu neemar derek mashal vedimyon bilbad vegam betirgume hattana"k kullo bishar leshonot shemmelammed lattinoqot yizzaher veyishmor bekamma debarim leharchiq hahagshama vekaasher timtza betargum uneqlos shemmosip millot betargum hammiqra kede leharchiq hahagshama veda ki timtza poh targum hammiqra bilshon arbi uleshon parse meyussad merabbenu seadya gaon veyesh bo kamma debarim metuqqanim heteb belashon arbi veazkir poh dabar echad asher bo teda yiqrat peninim shel hattargum hazzeh vehu ki pasuq "vayyinnachem Adonai ki asa et haadam baaretz vayyitatztzeb el libbo" (bereshit v, v) tirgem haggaon hannizkar "vetavvevadahum allah lamma tzannaham pi el eretz veotzel el mashqeh eli qelobaham" veken pasuq (bereshit v, z) "ki nichamti ki asitim" tirgem haggaon "ed tivvohadetehum kamma keliqqetaham" nimtza haggaon meparesh nechama miggezerat vaad sheggazar leadam moed uzeman qatzub velo sheyyichyeh leolam ki battechilla keshebbirem yada shessopam lachato velo epshar sheyyichyu leolam veqatzab lahem bemachshabto zeman mugbal sheyyihyu chayyim baaretz hallezu veken tirgem haggaon pasuq "veasu achika mitnachem leka leharegeka" (bereshit kz, mb) - "metoadak leyiqqatel" kelomar, qaba zeman veet laharigateka. ak targum pasuq "vehinnachem al haraa leammeka" (shemot lb, yb) tirgem haggaon tebat "vehinnachem" - "veatzpach" ayyen sham vehinneh mah shettirgem nechama leshon vv"d hu emet vekaka rauy laadam sheyyetargemu hamlammedim liladim vead lamadnu mittargumim shettirgem vayyitatztzeb el libbo deqae al haadam veha bearu nakon veken yizzaher hamlammed lehosip dabar betargum bishar leshonot kemo "veraita et achore" (shemot lg, kb) shettirgem haggaon "avvakar nuri" veken "vetassiteni bo" beiyyob (b, g) tzarik lehosip millat "demita" yaan ki ot v' shel tebat "vetassiteni" meshammesh bimqom tebat "demita" kemo "abiv veimmo" (shemot k, tv) deot va"v yeshammesh bimqom "o", veken pasuq "hannemalim am lo az, veyakinu baqqayitz lachmam" (mishle l, kh) deot va"v shel "veyakinu" meshammesh bimqom "ap al pi ken". veken "vaabadeka bau lishbar okel" (bereshit mb, y) avvat va"v meshammesh bimqom "abal" veken pasuq "ki haya aron haelohim bayyom hahu ubene yisrael" (shemuel  yd, ych) deot va"v shel "ubene" hu bimqom tebat "am" keillu katub im bene yisrael vekaelleh rabbot. ubederek zeh hitnaheg unqelos battargum shello, yishma chakam veyosip leqach:

clarification.explanation:
A children's teacher may not translate the Song of Songs into Arabic or other languages according to the plain meaning of the words alone, since the words of Song of Songs were not said in their plain sense at all, but were given only to be expounded — their plain meaning is metaphor and allegory. Therefore the author of the [Aramaic] Targum did not translate Song of Songs like other translations that render the words plainly, but brought midrashic commentary for each verse. And even in translating the rest of Scripture into other languages for teaching children, one must be careful and guard against several things to avoid anthropomorphism, as we find with Onkelos, who adds words in his translation of Scripture for this purpose.

Rabbi Yosef Chaim notes that there exists a translation of Scripture into Arabic and Persian established by our teacher Sa'adia Gaon, containing well-corrected matters, and cites one example demonstrating the "precious pearls" of this translation: the verse "and the Lord regretted that He had made man on earth, and He was grieved in His heart" — the Gaon translated "regretted" in the sense of "appointed time" — setting a fixed term and limited time: when the Holy One created man, He knew he would ultimately sin and could not live forever, and He set in His plan a limited time for him to live on earth; and he likewise translated "for I regret that I made them," and "and your brother comforts himself regarding you to kill you" — he set a time and season for your killing. But "and relent from the evil planned for Your people" he translated with a different term ("I will turn away"). The translation of "comfort/regret" in the sense of "appointed time" is correct, and teachers should translate this way for children; we further learn from his translation that "and He was grieved in His heart" refers to man — and this is a correct interpretation.

Likewise the teacher should be careful to add a word in translation where needed: "and you shall see My back" the Gaon translated "after My light" (the end of My light); and in the verse "and you incited me against him" in Job, one must add the word "as though," since the letter vav of "and you incited me" serves in place of this word. For the letter vav serves in Scripture in various meanings: in "his father and his mother" — in place of "or"; in "the ants, who have no chief, yet prepare their bread in summer" — in place of "nevertheless"; in "and your servants have come to buy food" — in place of "but"; and in "for the Ark of God was on that day, and the children of Israel" — in place of "with," as though written "with the children of Israel," and many such examples. And this is how Onkelos proceeded in his translation — "let the wise man hear and increase learning."
takeaways: Song of Songs should not be translated for children literally — it is entirely allegory meant only for exposition.
Every Scripture translation should guard against anthropomorphism, as Onkelos does by adding words.
"And the Lord regretted" is translated by Rav Sa'adia Gaon in the sense of a fixed, appointed time — the proper way to teach it.
The letter vav also serves in the sense of "or," "but," "with," or "nevertheless" — an explanatory word should be added in translation.
